title: A giant jigsaw
subtitle: Read the text below and think of the word which best fits each space. Use only one word in each space. There is an example at the beginning (0).
passage:
If you know anything about the wholesale warehouse chain, Costco, you'll know that it's a shop for people who are fans (0) OF the bulk buy. You can treat [[1]] to a 40-pack of toilet rolls, an 8-pound tub of popcorn and a 20-kilogram bag of basmati rice!

But, it's not just the home goods and food that are supersize. In actual [[2]], what's been dubbed as the 'world's largest puzzle' has recently [[3]] on sale in the store. The jigsaw box, in [[4]] you'll find a staggering 60,000 pieces, is a colourful collage of some of the world's most amazing places. Thankfully, for ease of construction, it can be broken [[5]] sixty sections of a thousand pieces each.

Not [[6]] will you need a lot of space (2.44 m x 8.84 m), but you'll also need a wad of cash. It will set you [[7]] over £500. So, only put this on your Christmas list if you have sufficient floor space and, perhaps more importantly, a relative [[8]] money to burn!

explanations.1: **Treat yourself to** — a fixed reflexive pattern: you buy something as a indulgence for yourself.
explanations.2: **In actual fact** — a set phrase meaning ‘really’ or ‘in reality’, introducing the surprising puzzle detail.
explanations.3: **Has gone / come on sale** — present perfect + on sale: the puzzle recently became available in the store.
explanations.4: **In which** — relative clause referring to the jigsaw box (where you find the pieces).
explanations.5: **Broken into / broken down into** — one-word gap before ‘sixty sections’: divide the puzzle into smaller parts for construction.
explanations.6: **Not only … but also** — correlative structure: you need space and a lot of money.
explanations.7: **Set you back** — phrasal verb meaning ‘cost you’ (here, over £500).
explanations.8: **A relative with money to burn** — **with** links the person to what they have (money to spend freely).
